utterances.text: Let us look at the next document on the same topic. That's 2D3039. Well, we'll see it. This is a record of issued items. Again, it's the BH Army. The date is the 29th of September, 1992. The weapons are delivered to the armed forces in Mostar, the 1st Mostar Brigade. Well, it's quite clear here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: And here we have a list of weapons. Could you please tell me, what kind of weapons are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are 84-millimetre, 60-millimetre mortars. Then there are shells for a 122-millimetre cannon, some rounds, so from the Central Logistics Base of the BH Army in Visoko. It was issued there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. And we have just one delivery note. That's document 2D3040. It pertains to the same factory. The date is the 30th of September, 1992. It's about the delivery of two different kinds of mortars, and as indicated above, it was -- the delivery was taken personally by Mirsad Cupina. "OS Mostar," that would be Armed Forces Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, here in court we have had a lot of debate in the course of the Stojic Defence case, and also when you showed some documents that pertained to the assistance to the BH Army, and those questions mostly focused, with the Prosecutor's objections, whether some weapons that were meant for Tuzla could have ended in some other place. And your answer was that there were no guarantees, there could have been no guarantees. But since this is of particular importance for the Defence, now I would like you to look at document 2D3036. Mr. Praljak, I think that you are familiar with this document. It is part of a document that you drafted. I don't want to confuse the Judges by telling them what document that is, but we need only this page. And please look at the date. Is the 22nd of March, 1993, and I'm deliberately now showing you this document from 1993. I will not be going back to 1992, just so that we can see how this process of arming went on. It says here: "The Supreme Staff of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, the Chief of Staff, Mr. Sefer Halilovic." This is from the commander, Rasim Delic, and he says: "I hereby submit a proposal for the unloading of the TMS which is supposed to head out from Zagreb, a total quantity of MTS reduced by 25 per cent, which was supposed to be taken by Croatia or in Grude." And then he goes on to say: "The assets for Tuzla would be partially brought back to Visoko upon their arrival in Tuzla in order to be distributed to the 3rd Corps and other units." And now it is indicated how the distribution would be actually done. Mr. Praljak, I'm not going to ask you whether you knew at the time about that, but I am asking you whether this document unequivocally shows that the assets that were supposed to reach Tuzla in March, due to this redistribution within the BH Army, actually were then headed to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, counsellor, let me say this clearly and so on. I've already said it a couple of times. First of all, the BH Army got 90 per cent of the overall weapons it had at least from Croatia and from the HVO throughout the war. Secondly, as soon as a convoy approved by anyone would cross the line and enter the territory controlled by the BH Army, the convoy went where the BH Army commanders wanted it to go. The Prosecutor's argument is that we distributed the weapons at will, saying, We'll give those that. But, of course, yes, sometimes we would write, This is for Gorazde, in Zagreb, when we heard all the moaning about where it was needed. But once it crossed the line, it was under the control of the BH Army, and they distributed the consignments as they saw fit. Now, perhaps some commanders might have complained, but it was their internal affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you have said this before. I just wanted to confirm that through some documents, because through the questions of the Judges I believe that it was not clarified fully. We have our next document, that's 3D1870, which shows this even more clearly. 3D1870. So this is a document from the 1st of April, 1993, and it originated from the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It says "Visoko Department." It was addressed to Mr. Sefer Halilovic, this request, and it says: "Attached to this document is a proposal for possible distribution of the MTS, materiel and equipment, that is to reach Pasalic or Tuzla." Mr. Praljak, well, here we see how the proposed distribution -- what is to go to the 1st Corps, the 4th Corps, 2nd Corps and 3rd Corps. I'm sorry, don't be mad with me, please. I'm just -- I just want you to tell me, once and for all. Could you please tell me whether this document clearly shows that the BH Army redistributed the assets that were sent in and that were supposed to reach Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Nozica and Your Honours, what would the 4th Corps in Mostar use to shoot at us? They did not have any defence industry. Even if we didn't have those documents, a logical question would be: What did they use to shoot at the HVO there? Weapons, and look at the quantities, RPG-7, that's seven and a half thousand, a total of seven and a half thousand. Well, they killed 500 of my soldiers with those RPGs, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, now regarding the previous document, let us look at how the assets headed out from Croatia so that we can establish a link and prove that the weapons came from Croatia. Let us look at 3D9 [as interpreted]. That's our next document. It's already exhibited. Let us just establish a link with the previous document. The 26th of March, 1993. The Zagreb Ministry of Defence issues an order for the issuing of the assets -- materiel and equipment for the purposes of the BH Army, through the Grude Logistics Base. And these are all the weapons that are listed in the previous document, 3D1870, where we can see that a proposal is made how to distribute it among the various corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you can see the quantities: the RPGs, seven pieces of -- seven and a half thousand, and also the rounds that are used by RPGs, 7 and 600.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 56, line -- where the number -- it's 17, 3D9, that's the way I heard the translation, but it is, of course, 3D00309.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document is 3D0009, just "9." I abridged it by dropping the 0s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But it has a different number written on its front page in our documents. There, it is "309." Oh, it says "3D," probably. Probably what looks like a 0 is a D, in fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This document is in e-court under that number. I can see it. Now you have me confused. And in e-court, it's precisely under this number that I used, but we can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Praljak, because of everything that has been said in the courtroom, I'm not going to talk about 1992, although it is quite relevant because the largest quantities were delivered from Croatia to the BH Army in 1992. But let us look at our next document which confirms this, and that's 2D3008. This is a report from the SIS. I don't know whether you had enough time to go through all the documents that you received.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is the assistant commander for security in the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. It's submitted to the assistant commander for security in the operational zone, Mr. Tomasevic. And now I'm interested in the first part. It says: "On the 31st of December, 1992, at 1600 hours, near the Novi Travnik firehouse, two trucks were noted, one of which was carrying a 122-millimetre howitzer, and the other one was carrying two mortars. We dispatched the military police patrol to check. The leader of the transport said that the equipment belonged to the 4th Corps and it was being transported from Visoko to Mostar. All the necessary documentation was in place." Signed by Mr. Petkovic and by Mr. Coric, and that these are the assets that were taken from the Bratstvo company in Visoko. And according to the documentation, it was likely transported to Mostar. Mr. Praljak, would it follow from this document not only that we have the paper trail, but we can see that this actually happened, that the assets were moved in this manner to Mostar, as we can see from the document 2D00577?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the 4th Corps and the 6th Corps had artillery, real artillery, and the assistant for artillery and shells and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Let us look at the next document. That's 2D197. Again, it's 1993. Have you been able to find it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's not in e-court, but we'll have it here. Again, this confirms our argument. This is the authorisation for the transportation of weapons for the needs of the BH Army to the Visoko Logistics Centre from Zagreb to Metkovic and then further on to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Praljak, I have to ask you this in this manner: Are these the weapons that were headed for Mostar to Posavina, or rather Tuzla, Posavina, or did they go to Visoko and then they were distributed as the BH Army decided?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are, for the most part, warm coats because it was winter-time, so it's military equipment and materiel for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Everything from uniforms to bullets went to Bosnia-Herzegovina from Croatia under the signature of some of the people present here in the dock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's now look at the next document, which is 2D3041. The date here is the 26th of March, 1993, the consignment order. It's a delivery of 7.62-millimetre bullets, and the goods will be taken over by Seta Sujab. Mr. Praljak, was this also for the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document is 2D3042. That's the 30th of March, 1993, once again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: And they are -- and it is MTS, and Seta Sujab is mentioned again, that name is mentioned again. And was this intended for the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly weapons for destroying bunkers, the Maljutka-type rockets and RPG-7 launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, which is 2D3043. The document is the 30th of March, 1993; that's the date. We have hand-held launchers, bullets for automatic rifles. 3D3043 [as interpreted] is the correct number, 3043. Have you found that, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was this MTS intended for the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 3.000 rifles, automatic ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just one more document and then I'll ask you some questions. 2D960 is the document number. My colleagues -- well, I seem to be a bit tired. The previous number was 2D3043. The last document is 2D960. The date is, once again, the 8th of March, 1993, and we're dealing with 630 bullets to be taken over by Sujab, Seta?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These aren't bullets. I can't see this very well, but it's artillery pieces, artillery shells. They're not really bullets, because the number's too few there. Can anybody see what it says?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, as far as I can see, it says "Bullet MTT364K-43." We'll zoom in there. There you go.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Petkovic -- it's not up to Petkovic to answer, but he could --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, we've zoomed in and it says --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, bullets refer to everything, but they're not bullets for rifles, they're something else. But never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Praljak, we've seen a number of consignment orders or delivery orders for weapons that were sent out from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia for the purposes of the BH Army. Now we're dealing with the beginning of 1993. Did you have any direct knowledge and information, in view of the posts you occupied, that these weapons were going to the BH Army, and whether you had any information whereby the BH Army did, in fact, receive those weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I took direct part in that. Not only did I have knowledge of it, but I was one of the people -- one of the few people who decided upon that. It was a state decision that had been taken in Zagreb, and this went on the whole time. How many more times do you need me to repeat that? Throughout the war, later on this was more difficult because we had to hide this from our own people later on, hide the fact that we were letting weapons go through to the BH Army. The situation was completely historically incomprehensible and very troubling. A commander letting ammunition and weapons go through to an army which was at the same time attacking him and his men is something that is incomprehensible, but that is the situation we found ourselves in, and despite that we seemed to be guilty and blamed for everything. That's incomprehensible. Nobody can understand that, and nobody else did that in the history of warfare except for the Croats, nobody else anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may ask a question. Mr. Praljak, do you think, retrospectively, that this was a good idea, to let all that through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, well, it was. In spite of everything, Your Honour. Had we not let it all through, Tuzla would have fallen, Gorazde would have fallen, Sarajevo would have fallen, Bihac would have fallen, and what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Fallen to whom, Mr. Praljak? To who would it have fallen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Into the hands of the Army of Republika Srpska, into Mladic's hands, and then you would have had two million more refugees leaving. The Muslims would have lost everything, the Croats would have lost, too, they would have lost out, and it would have been a complete catastrophe. This way, it was a lesser catastrophe. Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I've received a suggestion to the effect that this document, 2D960, was ammunition for a cannon of 150 millimetres, the M-43.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and that was a large number of rounds for that cannon. So they're not bullets, because it's for the 150 -millimetre cannon. But General Petkovic knows that much better than me because he's an artilleryman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we have seen a series of documents, and we've already seen many of them, but they do show formally that the Republic of Croatia sent weapons to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina via the HVO. Documents speak for themselves, but the question is different. Those weapons that were sent to the ABiH, were these weapons that were in the inventory of the Republic of Croatia or were these weapons that the Republic of Croatia bought outside its territory, but from other countries like the US, Germany, or whatnot, and that who were then sent to the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the spring of 1993, we would supply them with this. We would purchase it and gave it to them as an incentive for our joint struggle. Now, after that there was some flights coming in from other countries, and then we would let that through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Up until the spring of 1993, you say that these were weapons that you were buying abroad. Very well. The Republic of Croatia was operating with a budget, a yearly budget, like any other country. There are funds that are earmarked towards the Ministry of Defence, and each ministry gets a specific allocation; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partially, yes. But in the war, the Ministry of Defence has -- well, you can't calculate the budget. Yes, you can, you can say so many soldiers and so on and so forth, but as to the needs and requirements, they are determined by the Ministry of Defence budget and resources and funds. Now, Franjo Tudjman was complaining that we should reduce the army, that there should be mobilisation and so on, but we had to purchase weapons for Bosnia-Herzegovina and we had to run into debt, to be quite honest. We went to the commercial bank, a large bank, and we brought it to the brink of bankruptcy, to actual bankruptcy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're saying that you were just going into debt and borrowing from banks. Now, did the Croatian MPs know about this? Did they know that the Republic of Croatia was supplying the ABiH with weapons or was it done behind their back? Was it Mr. Tudjman and a small core of people, including you, who knew about this or was this done in the open, with the MPs knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole government certainly knew, the national unity government from 1992 to 1993, and later on the government presided over by Nikica Valentic. They knew fully what was going on. I can say with a great degree of certainty that 90 per cent of the MPs also knew. Probably not everybody knew what quantities were involved. Perhaps they didn't know about the quantities, except for the government, because the government knew about the quantities and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to have a follow-up question, and of course the issue of the arms transfer has been already many times treated here and discussed. And I would like to, as also my fellow Judges have done before me, to ask you about the following: When you answered first to the question raised by Judge Trechsel, you, among other arguments, you mentioned that if there wasn't this kind of arms transfer and cooperation with the BiH Army, then it was probably that region, I believe it was the Posavina, would have fallen into the Republika Srpska hands, and which would have resulted in two million more refugees. It is what you said, if I recollect properly. Now, my question is, therefore, as we already spoke about it before, that: That wasn't it characterised -- I mean, the arms transfer, couldn't it be characterised by, on your part, as choosing the lesser evil in that particular time and situation, and therefore you actually had done it with a view also to have your own interests met and defended, and it was, in other terms, if I may use this one, a kind of marriage of convenience that between the two parties you acted because of your interest, although you knew that it was also, to a certain degree, against your interests on another level? So it is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour Judge Prandler, our interests could have been quite simple; that I sit down with Mr. Karadzic, or that Petkovic sit down with Karadzic, and then we say, Listen here, Karadzic, 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina goes to you, we'll take 30 per cent. I'll turn the tap off, as far as the Muslims are concerned, and then a month later they will have to surrender because they won't have a single bullet. So that could have been the interest. And had that been our interest, then it would have been resolved in five minutes. He would have been satisfied with 70 per cent, and, to be quite frank, we could be quite pleased with 30 per cent. However, when you have dozens of people coming to Zagreb, hundreds of people coming to Zagreb, honest people, decent people, who were attacked from Gorazde, from Sarajevo, from Tuzla, from Bihac, Usora, who want to defend themselves, then you forget about politics for a time or reduce its significance, and you forget that in time those politics will turn against you. Well, it was a desire -- you can say "interest," but it was a desire. Well, if you look at anything in life and that what one does in life, it serves some interest. If you give somebody in the street a Euro, it makes you feel good, giving a beggar a Euro. But I can't characterise it that way. We did so for humanitarian reasons, humane reasons, state reasons. We wanted to have Bosnia-Herzegovina survive. We don't -- didn't want to have two million people on the move. We could have sent them to Hungary. Hungary was a mutual country. We were at war. We could have allowed them to go through a corridor and say, Here you are. So I don't think one can simplify matters in that way. When I and Mr. Stojic gave, say, half a million or a million marks worth of weapons to Sarajevo, I didn't even ask anyone. I didn't ask any of ambassadors or whoever whether they would approve that or not. There were people dieing over there, somebody was attacking them, and they're asking you to provide them with a truckload of weapons, and you do that, you give them a truckload of weapons without thinking about interests of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you that with all the questions -- you can see that the Judges are asking a lot of questions on this because we're at the very heart of this notion and concept of joint criminal enterprise, which is why the Judges are putting so many questions to try to see some light into this. If you allow me, I will envisage a situation under different angles; firstly, the presence of the Serbs jeopardising the very integrity of the Republic of Croatia. The Serbs are in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but they can very well attack and march on Zagreb, since they're already in Krajina. Now, seen from this angle, the Republic of Croatia has an interest in providing weapons to all those fighting the Serbs, with the idea of defending the territory -- the final idea of defending the territory of the Republic of Croatia, without taking into account the interest of the Croats living in Herzegovina. Do you believe that a reasonable politician or reasonable high-ranking military men might have been integrated in the political decision made by Mr. Tudjman, with the tacit agreement of his government, to send weapons to Bosnia and Herzegovina? Was this the main reason for supplying weapons, in order to make sure -- to preempt any attack from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honours, I'm grateful for any question you put to me, any. Let's be clear on that. When Milosevic realised that a Greater Serbia within the borders that he wanted was out of the question, and when Croatia was already a member of the United Nations, and when its borders were clearly defined, the only question remained was when we would be allowed to carry out an operation to liberate Croatia. Once the borders of Croatia were recognised and once Croatia became a member of the United Nations, the Serbs, in the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia, knew it in their minds that they had lost their war, that the war, as far as they were concerned, was over. The president of the state and the government allowed for the UNPROFOR to arrive in Croatia and for Slovenia to be reintegrated peacefully, just to show that we were against the war and that we could wait for years. Your Honours, we were prepared to liberate those areas even before, in military terms. Let's now start from this assumption: If we had an arrangement with Mladic to take 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to conquer Sarajevo and Srebrenica, not would they have attacked us, but they would have had a very easy time filling those areas with their own men, like they did with the area of Kosovo. And if we had been thinking along those lines, we would have resolved the situation sooner. You could see from the dozens of conversations that there was a desire to reach an agreement with Izetbegovic to organise Bosnia and Herzegovina and to allow Muslims to defend themselves. The cold political logic -- when I say "cold," I don't know what else to call it, maybe mathematically called "logic," would have certainly opted for another route. This was a principled consistent -- and principled policy, and that's why despite the RPGs and the shells for the 120-millimetre cannon were killing my own men, the men that I commanded in an area, and despite that the arms went on being shipped to Bihac, Tuzla, Gorazde, Sarajevo, well, we were hoping all that time that the leadership would finally understand that Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted only one thing, and that was an autonomy in the area that could have been 17 or 18 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, an area in which they were an absolute or relative majority, equal to anybody else, and that was all; nothing else, only that, and there were also some human connections. It is useless to try and explain everything in mathematical terms. For example, you have people who come to ask you for medicines, people who want to fight, and you cannot sit and watch them being killed. And despite of any politics that were in place, you give them weapons, even if you know that it may be turned against you, yourself, one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second aspect of my question -- I now see a different aspect. I saw the first. So the second aspect is this: Mr. Tudjman and all the members of the criminal enterprise, of which you are a part, that is, according to the Prosecution, know that to be successful with annexing the territory, there were only two ways of going about it; either invading the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was formerly Banovina from -- in 1929 to 1939, and then the international community is obviously going to be against it and, in fact, remember what the deputy secretary for defence said, Ralph Johnson, saying to Tudjman, that there had to be a final recognition given to the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or else hope on the part of the HVO that they would gain victories against the Muslims through military offensives - the 9th of May, the month of June, et cetera - and then the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, in the framework of a confederation with the Republic of Croatia, would achieve the dream of restoring Banovina. Now, in this second -- from this second angle, aspect, sending weapons, was there not a risk - and in fact Judge Trechsel asked you a question about this - was there not a risk that you would be reinforcing the fire-power of the Muslims and thereby preventing victories being gained by the HVO because, as you said yourself, the forces -- well, the ratio was 1:10, in terms of personnel, manpower, and we saw the documents proving that, and you give them arms, in spite of there being 10 times more of them, and it seems to be totally unreasonable? So what do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think what you're saying is correct, and I suggest that the Trial Chamber brings in a psychologist who would test my IQ. But how can you want to conquer something? Well, let's put it this way: In 1992, after the conquests in East and West Mostar, all it took was to disarm or not allow any kind of establishment of the BiH Army. All it took was for somebody to say, Here you have the HVO, well, they're much stronger then. And it was at that particular time, you saw it, weapons -- well, Luburic, you saw him. I had Luburic distributing the insignia among them, and I had created the insignia myself in Zagreb. He was my commander in Capljina. The population returned to Stolac, and we trained and armed their brigade in Stolac; and all that in order to carve a piece of their territory. Your Honours, do you really think that we are that kind of idiots? Not even a cat would think along these lines. I really can't comprehend this. Let's put it in a nutshell. There was no -- nothing of that sort. Towards the -- 1992, there were those soldiers, and for five months later, I was -- let me not mention his name, the gentleman's name, although his name is public. Of course, in the Parliament, we were sending a delegation to say, Please calm the situation down. We were running all over Central Bosnia. We were making suggestions of a joint command. We pushed it to the limits. I took -- I grovelled up to those men to ask them to do something normal finally. Only when they lost in an attack against us, when they did not realise their goals, it was only then when the normal way of thinking about the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina started. If they had succeeded, then take my word for it, what you are saying -- what the international community and the Americans said, all of them adjusted day in day out to the prevailing military situation on the ground. The fact that what the Z-4 group was offering to the Serbs in Croatia as a national minority right is not even 10 per cent of the rights that they enjoy in the Croatian state where they are a constituent people. That's as regards the international community. All they cared about was for the pictures and images not to be shown on the news from Bosnia and Herzegovina as they were. As for the principles, please, Your Honours, let's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will two more documents which will round off the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: But before that, Mr. Praljak, I would like us to go back to the questions --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say this: In that Z-4 plan Mr. Grbak [phoen], who was sitting here, was offering the Serbs a judiciary in Croatia, elections, parliament, money, a state in a state, and they were rebels at the time and they were a national minority. And Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who are a constituent and sovereign people, there's no cat's chance in hell to have all that, because that would be contrary to some other interests that prevailed there. And there you have him talking -- speaking about principles. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, just for a moment let's discuss a few more details. You said that people came from Bihac, Tuzla, Sarajevo, Gorazde, and they wanted an opportunity to defend themselves. We've shown a document today, which is 2D3008, which shows clearly that the HVO, in the month of January 1993 - that's the SIS report, you don't have to look for it - provided their concern for the arrival weapons for the 4th Corps. Please allow me to put my question to you. I would kindly ask you to explain to the Trial Chamber what -- which operations were conducted before the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993 jointly by the BiH Army and the HVO against the Serbs, and whether that was the reason why you and those who were decision-makers at the time delivered weapons to the BiH Army, was you had a common military objective. What I mean by that is Mostar, in the summer of 1992, Jajce, the Operation Bura, and other operations.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not like that, Ms. Nozica. We did have our joint operations, but if I had wanted to keep two howitzers for myself, then I could have given them to my own crews, not to the BiH Army. Bura was primarily an HVO operation. The fact that some small BiH Army units participated in it was negligible. There were Muslim soldiers as members of the HVO, but that was primarily an HVO operation, and I was not obliged to provide howitzers and mortars to another army if I didn't want to do so. I could have kept them for myself. I could have told them, If you have a crew for that operation, you can give us our crew and we will carry out a joint operation, but the howitzers would remain on my inventory list. Petkovic, Stojic, and everybody else thought that the arming of the BiH Army would create the joint armed forces of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., the BH Army and the HVO, which would have a joint command and plan operations together. That's why we acted the way we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, this is exactly what I asked you, sir. I asked you about the joint military, and I'm happy with your answer because it answered my question. But just one more question about that topic. When His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you about the money and the justification for the government, can you tell us whether you know anything about the immigrants hailing from Bosnia and Herzegovina paying a considerable amount of money and that Croatia used those resources for the purchase of weapons that was then channeled towards the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In percentage terms, not in absolute terms because there are not that many Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in percentage terms the biggest number of people working abroad were Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And again in percentage terms, the highest numbers were Herzegovinians. Half of the Herzegovinians were working abroad because Herzegovina is a very poor region, and after the Second World War nothing was being built or manufactured there, and they were the ones who paid most money because they wanted to be the masters of their own destiny, they wanted freedom. And all that was channeled into the joint budget and Minister Susak had it at his disposal, and, therefrom, the resources for purchasing weapons, and they paid much more money than Croatia gave us weapons, according to my modest estimates, but I can't be 100 per cent sure that my estimates are absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now let's look at two more documents just briefly. If you look in your pink binder, and you can also rely on the e-court, where you will see the document immediately, the document number is 2D01251. This is a letter sent to Mr. Susak which was written by Mr. Jelavic, and on the 1st of May -- March 1993, and provides an overview of the MTS confiscated by the BiH Army, the MTS that had been sent for Central Bosnia. The quantity is huge. Do you know, Mr. Praljak, that such things did, indeed, happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: At the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: And this is the time, as we have seen, when the arms were sent from Zagreb for the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there were also attacks, and at that time there were raids, and the team in Zenica, who was in charge of the entire area, and the Mujahedin, had already in place a clear plan as to what they wanted to do. I was there in the month of March. There are documents testifying to that. There are some things that were written at some meetings. This was an attempt on my behalf to calm the situation down. The Vance-Owen agreement was signed. However, when I saw the situation on the ground, when I saw the appearance of Travnik and the 7th Muslim -- and the 17 brigades, then I realised that the story was over and that it was just a matter of time when the HVO would be in -- just erased from the face of the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now let's look at another document in your pink binder. This is 2D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, when we look at the document 2D01251, if I've understood you properly, where apparently this is also intended for the ABiH, well, at the end of this document we see that food is being mentioned: cheese, 1.200 kilos; sugar, 2.050; spaghetti, beans, and so on. So this food, was it intended for the HVO, for the ABiH, or for both?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I do apologise. If I may, it's my document, and then I made a mistake. Your Honour, it says "Proposal: Review of the MTS seized by the BH Army."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to cut a long story short, they stole it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: And it was sent to the Central Bosnia Operational Zone from Croatia; is that so, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They stole it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake. Let me correct it. This document was sent to Mr. Susak in Croatia, and the document was signed by Mr. Jelavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: He was the assistant chief for logistics in the Main Staff at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is HVO logistics. They sent it to the HVO in the Operational Zone Central Bosnia, and the army stole it, full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please look at 2D0008 [as interpreted]. It's in the pink folder.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, this is a report about materiel and military equipment that the BH Army, in February 1993 -- 2D00008. So that's four 0s and then 8.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: So it's four 0s. So this transport was stopped. It was humanitarian aid for Gorazde-Merhamet. And when search was conducted, it was determined that in addition to the humanitarian aid, there was a double-bottom concealing a huge quantity of weapons. This document has already been exhibited, but I remember that at one point when I was showing this document, you intervened saying -- I heard you say - I don't know whether it was on the transcript - that you were familiar with some of the circumstances regarding this weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of this case. I was informed about it. Well, it was simply unclear why, in addition to everything that we were giving to them, they were also smuggling the weapons in. They could have obtained a "laissez passer" for all of it, authorisation to pass. So in addition to all the authorisations and all the signatures that they got, they used humanitarian aid convoys to smuggle weapons in. If they didn't have the requisite papers, then the military police would stop them and seize the transports. But I think that in the end, they got them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that you said that they got all the weapons back. This was the gist of your intervention. Mr. Praljak, this completes this topic. Can we now make a break, and then I would like to embark on a new topic which will be a lengthy one, so I don't want to start before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, it was high time for us to take our break. Let's now take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Praljak signaled me across the courtroom that he wishes to raise an issue before I continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not that I wanted to raise an issue. I just wanted to add something to what I said previously. The first thing would be about the distribution from the Bratstvo company in Travnik. I mediated in that situation, and the Croatian Army bought from Bratstvo a certain number of coastal cannons that could not be used anywhere else but at the places where the Croatian coastline was to be defended. A Bratstvo delegation came to Zagreb, and the cannons were bought to provide the Bratstvo employees with work and money. My second remark is about the weapons in Merhamet, and now -- just now I've remembered those weapons were photographed. I remember it well, and I was the one who asked from Mr. Stojic and Valentin Coric and others to let those through. The weapons were photographed, and I believe that the people spent a day and or a night there. They were questioned. And then on the following day, the convoy with the humanitarian aid and weapons continued on the journey; the following day or the day after. I don't know how long they stayed. And these would be my two remarks, following your question and following what I already said. MS. NOZICA [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, let me just say something. The last remark refers to document 2D8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Praljak. I listened to what you were saying, and I would like to put a question to you. The two drivers of the truck were interrogated. We have a copy of their hearing. One is called "Zanovic [phoen], Zenal," and he says that he had papers for this illegal weapons transport. At least that's what he claims. So if he had the necessary documents for this weapons transport, this must mean that the Croatian authorities, i.e., the Republic of Croatia, knew that these weapons were to be supplied to the Muslims, but that they would be transported under the cover of a humanitarian aid transport; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have that information at the time, to be quite frank. But if that's the statement that they gave, well, I don't know, although at that time it was indicated that they had only for humanitarian aid, not for weapons. But to be quite frank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, take a look at the hearing by this Hasanovic person in your own language, the three last lines. He seems to say that he had the right -- necessary documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It says here, I transported weapons earlier, but then earlier I had the papers for the transport of weapons, which was not done this time. So at that point in time he did not have the relevant paperwork for the transportation of weapons, but he had done that before, and on those previous occasions he had had paperwork. I don't know how this is translated into English, but he did not have the necessary paperwork for the transportation of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in English, it said: "But at that time --" he said earlier, he says it's earlier. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read the sentence in Croatian, and I quote: "I transported weapons on earlier occasions." But at that time, when he was transporting weapons at that time, "I had paperwork necessary to legally transport the weapons, and on this time -- and this time, this was not done. I claim that I was not given any information, was not aware of anything, and as for all those weapons, only Suad Sagolj, Riza Bukvica [phoen], and Sefer Omerbasic would be the right persons to talk about it." So they organised the loading of the weapons without saying anything to the drivers and without giving the drivers the appropriate paperwork permissions. They did not submit a request for this permit to be issued and signed by whoever was -- had the right to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, I looked at the translation, and it is indicated that in the past, this person had had the paperwork. But at any rate, it's clear now that Mr. Praljak read it out for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Praljak, I would like us to move to a topic that we could call "Bosnian Posavina." Could you please look at document 3D1699.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: 3D1699. This is a document that was shown to you in your examination-in-chief. It's a memo from Mr. Tus to Mr. Tudjman. Just a very brief introduction and then I'll be asking you some questions about things that are contentious in this document. And he says that from the commander of the Slavonian theatre, he received a report which is forwarded in its entirety because of its contents, and then he goes on to say: "Please confirm or modify the task that the command of the Slavonian theatre has been given." So at the beginning of this report that is forwarded in its entirety, it was drafted by Mr. Petar Stipetic, it's your document and you're quite familiar with it, the date is the 29th of October, 1992, and it says here: "Report about contact with the coordinator of the Bosnian Posavina HVO and the presidents of the Supreme Command of the BH Army." And it says at the beginning that a new coordinator has been appointed of the Bosnian Posavina HVO, Mr. Ivankovic, and that a meeting was held with the representatives of the BH Army. But what I'm interested in is the first passage, the last sentence, where it says: "I was also told by him that Mr. Stojic is expected to arrive any day now from the HVO Main Staff," the Main Staff of the Herceg-Bosna HVO, "as the military coordinator for this area, who will be authorised to reorganise the command and units in the Bosnian Posavina HVO." Mr. Praljak, since you testified about all the positions that Mr. Stojic held from the time of your arrival, and even before that, could you please tell Their Honours whether Mr. Stipetic obviously shows his ignorance of what Mr. Stojic was doing and that Mr. Stojic was obviously not any kind of coordinator for the Bosnian Posavina area at that time or at any point in time later?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not the coordinator, but I do know that at this time Mr. Alija Izetbegovic did visit the command in Slavonski Brod and that on that occasion he asked how long the HVO could hold on in that area, offering that he would go to Sefer Halilovic and ask for some brigades to be dispatched to that area, which shows either complete ignorance of the military situation or something else, but it really makes no sense whatsoever. Unfortunately, Bosnian Posavina, apart from its small part, was lost soon afterwards, well, precisely because -- well, for a variety of reasons, because the Republika Srpska Army was very strong there, much stronger than the HVO units, and this corridor was of vital importance for Banja Luka and so on, and because the 2nd Corps of the BH Army didn't exert any pressure from the bottom section or from the east to help the HVO in their difficult defence of this area which lasted for months with a logistics support from the Croatian Army in some sort of coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: This document talks about the OOG, Operational Group Bosnian Posavina, and the setting up of a number of brigades in Bosnian Posavina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' note: We did not catch the numbers because of the speed at which counsel is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know who were members of these brigades, in terms of their ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of these brigades is linked with a specific location. 101 is from Bosanski Brod; 102 is from I don't know where; 103 is from Derventa, and so on and so forth, and there were Croats and Muslims in their ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You may not have heard this, Ms. Nozica. I'm speaking to you, not to the witness. The interpreters have complained they did not hear what document you were talking about, and therefore we did not learn either. The reason was speed, they said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The numbers of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the document is already in the transcript. It's document 3D01699. It's in e-court. We have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, apparently I have also misunderstood. It's the numbers of the brigade that they did not understand, the numbers of the brigade that you have --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me just repeat. It says in the document, we can see in the transcript, 101st, 102nd, 103rd. Yes, we have it. I think I'm speaking really clearly now, and 105th Brigade of the HVO, 105. Yes, now it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, now I would like you to look at 2D1262. That's our next document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Has it been recorded that 101 was from Bosanski Brod, 103 was from Derventa, and that the brigades were set up on a territorial basis, as was the usual practice in the HVO? Each location had its own brigade, if there were enough people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is now in the transcript, we can see on this page, lines 13, 14, 15 and 16. So the document is 2D1262. Mr. Praljak, these are minutes from the 5th session of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, held on the 17th of October in Travnik. In the course of the examination by my learned friend Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' note: Could all the microphones that are not in use be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: -- regarding the HVO's -- or, rather, the communities of Herceg-Bosna and Usora, he asked whether the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna ever accepted those communities. This document -- well, several pages are already exhibited, page 1 listing persons who were at the session of the Presidency, but now I would like you to look at page 15 in the Croatian version. That would be page 2D79-0056. We'll find it. Yes, that's right. So if we could go back to page 15 in e-court, because we have page 16 in Croatian. And in the English version, we have -- yes, that's right, page 16. We have item number 18, "Examination of the Decisions on Joining the Unified HZ-HB by Croatian Communities of Bosnian Posavina, Central Bosnia and Usora." Mr. Praljak, we can see here that Bozo Vilusic from Tuzla was the first to take the floor, and he informed those present that in North-Eastern Bosnia, in Tuzla to be more specific, a Croatian Defence Council was set up and the Croatian Community of Sole, and that for objective reasons they have been unable to submit their application for membership, and now they would like to join the unified HZ-HB. And he also reports that the municipalities of Banovici, Lukavac and Zivinice were part of this community. And in the community of Sole -- well, rather, we have already talked about this community. And now I would like you to look, after this intervention, at page 16 in the Croatian text. It's the very end, and that's 2D79-0057 in the English version, the last part of this intervention, where it says: "Proposal for the joining into the unified HZ-HB of the communities of Bosnian Posavina, Usora, Central Bosnia, the community of Sole, Sarajevo, has been adopted unanimously." Mr. Praljak, Mr. Karnavas showed you two documents that pertained to the community of Usora whereby it exceeds the HZ-HB, and let me say for the transcript that this is document 1D2255, and the decision on the accession of Central Bosnia, that's 1D2252. Mr. Praljak, did you know that all those communities that are listed here at the session of the Presidency on the 17th of October in Travnik actually acceded to the HZ-HB, joined it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I learned later. I didn't know that at the time when decisions were adopted, but later on I learned that by talking to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, now I'm going to be torturing you a little bit, but I think it would be logical to do so. Could you please look at the map that Mr. Karnavas showed you. That's 1D2843. You made some markings. You drew in Central Bosnia and Usora. 1D - yes, it's in the record - 2843. If we could please have that map. Let us try and mark the communities which you did not mark last time, the community of Sole, Bosnian Posavina, and Sarajevo. Yes, we have it here. And in this document, it is indicated that Banovici, Lukavac and Zivinice shall comprise the community of Sole, together with Tuzla, so I would like to ask you if you could just mark those locations. I wanted to show you a document -- a map of the HZ-HB, but unfortunately that map does not have the names of other towns indicated, and it would be very difficult for us to find those, too. So we're looking for Tuzla, Lukavac, Banovici and Zivinice.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't seem to be working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mean your pen? Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not working. Something seems to be happening with our technical facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I come back, Your Honours, to that document tomorrow morning, if this -- which will give the technicians time to resolve this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can it not be done on the ELMO? Is there no paper copy of this map?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't have that on the ELMO because Mr. Praljak was working with the electronic document, so I wanted to apply the same system and procedure throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you mark in now? If not, we'll do it tomorrow morning. I'll have it printed out. Never mind. I'll print the map out and we'll come to that tomorrow and place it on the ELMO. But, anyway, staying with that same topic, Mr. Praljak, you confirm that these communities that we mentioned, including Bosanska Posavina, in October 1992 came within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Praljak, here in court, on the 11th of February, 2009, we had Mr. Stipo Buljan here as a witness. He worked in the Operation Zone of Bosanska Posavina. And on pages 36759 of the transcript, to 36766 of the transcript, he spoke about documents 2D00605 and in continuation until document 2D00624, he addressed those pages, he spoke about the national -- the ethnic composition of the HVO units in Bosanska Posavina, and the HZ-HB took care of those. Now, these documents, the documents that we put to Mr. Buljan and were admitted into evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or, rather, were not admitted into evidence, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because they were lacking a piece of information, they were lacking the dates when these individuals were killed or wounded, so let's now take a look at the next document -- yes. The usher was so good as to print out the map for us, so maybe we could go back to that now. And we were looking for Tuzla. Banovic, Lukavac, from Zivinice.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tuzla, 1; Sarajevo, 2; Zivinice, 3; Banovic, 4; Lukavac, 5, and Posavina, 6, these areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit IC1034. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, would you now take a look at the next document, which is 2D01561, the next in order.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have it on e-court as well, or we will do in just a moment. Now, Mr. Praljak, this is a letter from the County of Posavina, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 7th of May, 2009. And at the request of the Stojic Defence and pursuant to a Trial Chamber decision about the non-admittance of the documents, Mr. Buljan asks that this be supplemented -- the document be supplemented with additional information about the killing and wounding of HVO members in this area. So, Mr. Praljak, would you now please tell the Court whether you know, and I've already asked you about this, but as an introduction to the following documents, do you know or did you have contacts with and do you know that in all these units there were members of both ethnicities and that they were casualties and fatalities, too, and that the numbers were similar, and that the HZ-HB took care of them, as Mr. Buljan said during his testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there, too, in the fighting over there for some 10 to 12 days at the beginning of July 1992, and I am fully versed with the situation, both then and later on. So there was a mixed ethnic composition, Croats and Muslims. There were even some Serbs, a few in number as far as I remember. But, anyway, and the casualties and fatalities was extremely high in the area, because there was fierce fighting. The Army of Republika Srpska, well, it was vital for their survival, this area, so the fighting was fierce, and the number of killed and wounded in all the brigades, or almost all of them, were high, extremely high, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'd like now to go back to something. I'd like to show you those 20 documents. So could you tell us whether you know which the units were? And you mentioned some of them a moment ago. So take a look at the first of those documents, which is 2D1541, yes, 1541. This is a list of fatalities among the HVO from the Bosanski Brod municipality who were Croats, and it's the 101st HVO Brigade. Now, you said, Mr. Praljak, that they were determined by territory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that brigade, I knew its -- who its commander was. I took part in the fighting for a time, and I know that there were exceptionally high fatalities not only in that brigade, but others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, the column on the date of the fatalities confirms what you said, that most of them were in 1992, most of the people killed were killed in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next page. 2D82-0055 is the number. That is the Croatian version, and in English it's simpler. But, anyway, they are the killed HVO members from the Bosanski Brod municipality who were Bosniaks, of Bosniak ethnicity; is that right? So the Croatian fatalities are shown first, and then we have the Bosniaks next?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 221 Croats and - how many here? - 101 Muslims or Bosniaks, whatever you like to call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Praljak. And my questions will be the same for the next documents, and the next one is 2D1542. These are the fatalities in the HVO for Orasje, and we have the Croats first, and it is the 106th HVO Brigade from Orasje. Did you know that brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When it comes to this brigade, Ms. Nozica, you must bear in mind the fact that it managed to retain control of part of Bosanska Posavina, the territory, and the number -- and it continued to fight, so the number of fatalities was even higher. And there were a lot of people who were killed after 1992 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, and we can see that if we look at the dates, leafing through the dates of the fatalities. We have 1994 and 1995 even. Now take a look at page 2D82-0069 now, please, where we have a list of members of the brigade who were Bosniaks, of Bosniak ethnicity, and who were killed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a lot fewer Bosniak fatalities there, for the simple reason that at that time many who had survived and were wounded had gone to Croatia and were refugees there, and Orasje itself was defended by larger numbers of Croats than Muslims than was the case previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we can look at 2D01543. That's the next document, and these are the fatalities from the Bihac municipality of Croatian ethnicity. And the unit's name was ZM Bihac. And we have the Croats listed first, and on 2D82-0079 we have the Bosniaks listed. And if you remember, Mr. Buljan said that in this operation zone, there were parts of other brigades, and he mentioned the Bihac Brigade as being one such?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a small number of Croats and not a very large HVO unit in Bihac. Well, for that small brigade, a lot of Croats were killed, fewer Muslims in the HVO, because the BH Army over there had an entire corps and there weren't many Muslims in the Croatian brigade. And I'd like to mention in that regard that the commander, himself, of that unit, the HVO unit in Bihac, later on, under very -- his name was Santic, and he was killed not on the battle-field but in the rear, after a meeting with the BH Army, under unexplained circumstances, which led to quite a problem, and the circumstances of his death have not been elucidated to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at 2D01544, please, which is a list of HVO members who were killed of Brcko municipality, Croats killed. This is the 108th HVO Brcko Brigade. I'll just show you the page which lists the Bosniaks. There are far fewer of them once again, and that is page 2D82-0086.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This brigade was completely mutilated. Only if you have such great losses would you not be affected, if you had a marine's brigade or a foreign legion brigade, but these were extremely large fatalities for such a small brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now look at 2D01545, please, and here it says HVO fatalities who were Croats in Derventa municipality. And that was the -- let me repeat the number, 2D01545 is the document number, the page number, and it was the 103rd HVO Derventa Brigade, a large brigade. First of all, we have the Croats who were killed, and then on 2D82-0099 we have listed the Bosniak fatalities. And here we can see, Mr. Praljak, something very interesting, and you can testify about that. These were fatalities in 1992 mostly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could tell you what the battle-front looked like at the period of time when I was there. 270 fatalities in a brigade of that type, well, that is an extremely high number, extremely high losses. They were decimated, in the true sense of the word. And what it looked like over there, well, let's leave that alone and let's count the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, we are in a position to have to do that now, so take a look at the next document, which is 2D01546, once again the list of HVO dead for Modrica municipality. It is the 105th HVO Brigade of Modrica, and on page 2D82-0110 - that's the right number - we have the Bosniak fatalities. The 105th Modrica Brigade is the one we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing to add here, Madam Nozica. This was the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was a joint defence set up by the Croats and Muslims jointly. Croatia offered complete logistical support, because otherwise they wouldn't have been able to survive, and it resulted, unfortunately, apart from loss of territory, there was loss of life, too. Had a normal relationship existed and ratio of forces existed throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, the situation wouldn't have been as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, can we now take a look at document 2D1547, where we see the Croatian fatalities for Odzak municipality. It was the 102nd Odzak Brigade, and on page 2D82-0121 we have the list of HVO Bosniak dead, 41 of them. Did you know that this brigade existed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, we heard from Mr. Buljan that the HZ-HB took care of some other brigades in the area, so now take a look at 2D01548, the next document, please, which is a list of HVO dead for Tuzla municipality; Croats. And it was the 115th HVO Brigade called Zrinski from Tuzla, and we've already mentioned that during this trial, and on page 2D82-0131 you have the names of the dead who were Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yet further proof that the HZ -- or the Croats, in fact, defended Bosnia and Herzegovina and that they did this with great loss of life and suffering. So there's no sense in talking about a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and an agreement on that between Milosevic and Tudjman, and then to have so many people dying in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And these dead people, these people killed, are best proof and evidence of how the Croats behaved, both in political terms and in military terms, when it came to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: And could you now look at 2D1549. This is the 107th Brigade of the HVO in Gradacac. Were you aware of the existence of this unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But let's look at the number of fallen Bosniaks in the 107th Gradac Brigade. There were 245 of them. 245 Bosnian Muslims were killed in an HVO brigade, which was the 107th Brigade, and there were some 70 or 80 Croats altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, I have no comment. The document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you now look at 2D1550. This is a list of casualties in Bosanski Samac, first the Croats, and the first brigade listed is 104th Brigade, and then the 105th Brigade. You've already told us that the lists are segregated by the places. Could you now look at 2D82-0153?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are Muslims, Bosniaks, who were killed in this HVO brigade. There were 24 of them, and at the time there were Croats -- unfortunately, we are counting the dead, segregated by their ethnicity, but in the face of such indictment this is all we are left to do. There are 152 people who died. Unfortunately, there are no military experts who would be able to tell you how great a loss this is for amateurs -- military amateurs who, until a day or two days before that, were common civilians who rose up to defend their country. And here you see thousands of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: We are now moving on to something less gruesome, which is the list of people who were wounded in the war. Mr. Buljan testified about the care extended to the families of the fallen and the wounded that the HZ-HB was in charge of. Now could you please look at 2D01551. We will use the same methodology. First, we are looking at Bihac and the list of the wartime military invalids from Bihac, and now on page 2D82-0162 we have Bosniaks who were also invalids?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Bihac, which was predominantly inhabited by the Muslims, there were people, Bosniaks, who were simply members of the HVO, and I claim for all of these documents that there was never a distinction made based on the ethnicity of the wounded and the dead, either in the HVO or in Croatia. And, for example, when I went to the hospital to take the cigarettes to the wounded, I never made any distinction between the wounded. There were people lying there without legs and other extremities, and I distributed cigarettes among them equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now we are moving on to Bosanski Brod. First Croats, the document number is 2D1552. There's a large number of invalids both of Croatian and Bosniak origin, and the list of Bosniaks starts with the page number 2D82-0175. This is the 101st HVO Brigade of Bosanski Brod. We've already spoken about it, but now we are talking about invalids.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can I say? There's nothing to say but that these numbers are terrible, so many invalids among the Croats; 150 Muslims, even more among the Croats. They had fought together, together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, on the other hand, if anywhere we could have imposed our own will or make distinctions, that could have been it, because of the vicinity of Croatia, but no distinctions were ever made from the perspective of Croatian politics. The territory was defended jointly, by joint forces, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Document 2D01553 is a list of military invalids of the Bosanski Samac municipality, first Croats, and the numbers speak about the 104th Brigade, and we have Bosniaks on page 2D82-0191.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 345 Croats, or 363, rather, and there are 32 Muslims. However, look, there are also people here who had come, for example, Bernard Hans Pater [phoen], Marijan Kobalid [phoen], who had come to see me in Zagreb, people from Europe, from all over Europe. Of course, among them there was a number of dogs of war, as one would call them, but a number of them simply came to fight, to assist people who were fighting. And I felt sorry, when I was leaving the military, that the lists of those people were not maintained, because there were a couple of them who had committed crimes and were criminals, and that's why nobody cared about maintaining contacts with the rest of them to thank them and to acknowledge them and tell them how we respected them. Unfortunately, later on there was a desire to tarnish the image of the war and for everybody to be proclaimed criminal. Although, statistically speaking our war was not worse than any other war before or after. However, that war was proclaimed as a war that was -- that involved only criminals. But certainly not so many people would have been killed if all were thugs and hooligans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: There were a lot of national minorities in that area in the north. It was famous, in the former Yugoslavia, as the territory inhabited by a large number of national minorities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, and the situation has changed drastically since.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm saying this because of some names which may be unusual when compared to the names or, rather, last names of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you now please look at 2D01554. This is the 108th Brigade of the HVO in Brcko, which also had a number of Croatian military invalids. Could you please look at 2D82-0204, to look at the Bosniak war invalids.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's nothing to say here. Actually, the number of killed and wounded was proportionate to the national structure of the brigade, because these people were -- fought together and were wounded together. The number of wounded and killed reflects the national breakdown of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak, that I am exposing you to looking at all of these documents, but there's no other way for me to either confirm or not confirm this. The only way I can do it is to introduce documents through witnesses, and you are somebody who knows about these documents.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, Ms. Nozica. I can tell you that I have looked at all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, we have another ten minutes, and we will complete this exercise within the next ten minutes. The next document is 2D01555. This is a list of military invalids in Derventa, first Croats. This is the 103rd Brigade of the HVO in Derventa. You already said that you're familiar with that brigade. And the list of military war invalids of Bosniak ethnicity starts on page 2D82-0219.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the document. Nothing to add. Huge numbers. There's nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Document number 2D01556. This is a list of the HVO invalids in Gracac municipality, again first Croats, the 107th Gracac Brigade. And then on page 2D82-0231, we have members of the RVA [as interpreted] of Bosniak ethnicity. We've already spoken about these brigades, have we not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next one is 2D1557. This is the 105th HVO Brigade in Modrica, and the first list is -- represents Croats. And then on 2D82-0236 are Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And again this reflects the national composition of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have three more documents. The first one is 2D01558, the 102nd Brigade, Odzak. The first list is of members of that brigade of Croatian nationality, and then on page 2D82-0247 gives Bosniak members of that Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now could you please look at 2D1559. This the 106th Brigade of the HVO in Orasje, and it also had a huge number of war invalids, both Croats as well as Bosniaks, and the Bosniaks are on page 2D82-0276. You've already spoken about them.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orasje fought until the very end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Orasje was that part that managed to defend itself thanks to a good state of organisation, a good commander, less interference from some political structures in the area. In any case, for them the war lasted for much longer than for some other brigades that pulled out from the territory in the north and for other brigades that remained as elements of the Tuzla Corps and was engaged throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, this is shown or is reflected in the list and in the dates when people were wounded, because we can see the years 1992, 1993, 1994 and -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: And, finally, the Tuzla municipality, invalids of Croatian origin. The document number is 2D1560. There is first a list of Croats. Luckily enough, the number is somewhat lower. And then page number 0289, Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was somewhat fewer Bosniaks in the HVO because the BH Army was fighting very close to them, so I suppose that most of them joined the BiH Army. But many of them never left the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, my final question covering all the documents that I've just shown you: Do you confirm that it is true that all of these units were of mixed ethnic composition, and do you know that, as you've told us, but just in conclusion, that the families of the fallen soldiers, irrespective of their ethnicity, the HVO was looking after those families all that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the HVO and the Croatian state as a whole. The number of wounded and fallen was certainly very high. I am aware of that. I knew it at the time, and I knew it after the operations. And as far as the HVO and the Croatian state are concerned, no distinction was ever made among these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Praljak. Your Honours, I would like to move on. And instead of starting it today, could we please stop working for today and continue tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, as far as the time you have, I must tell you that you've already used up three hours so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... I would like to say this because of my learned friend who follows me. I would kindly ask you to approve the 45 minutes which I am entitled to, because one hour is simply not going to be enough to do everything I planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you know, the hearing will be taking place tomorrow afternoon. We shall meet here again at a quarter past 2.00 tomorrow. So have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of June, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: [The accused Prlic and Coric not present]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
